questions.q: Who among the following abolished ‘Dual Government’ system in Bengal ?
questions.explanation: In 1771, the Court of Directors decided to end the Dual Government system. This decision was implemented in 1772 by Warren Hastings. The Calcutta Council and its President were instructed to act as the Diwan themselves and take over the administration of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Warren Hastings removed the two Deputy Diwans, Muhammad Raza Khan and Raja Shitab Rai, from their posts. Under the Dual Government system, which is considered to have begun in Bengal from 1765, the Company retained the Diwani rights and carried out the Nizamat functions through the Nawab; however, the real power remained with the Company. Clive believed that all power lay with the Company and that the Nawab had only a shadow of authority. He wrote to the Select Committee: “This name, this shadow is necessary, and we should accept it.”

questions.q: The first railway in India was laid down during the period of-
questions.explanation: The first railway line was laid in 1853 between Bombay and Thane during Dalhousie’s time. The first passenger train of Eastern India ran on 15 August 1854 between Howrah and Hooghly.

questions.q: Which of the following social reforms were started by William Bentinck? 1. Abolition of Sati Pratha 2. Abolition of slavery 3. Removal of the provision of disqualification due to religious conversion 4. Suppression of organized gangs of thugs Select the correct answer from the code given below-

options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: Lord William Bentinck became the Governor-General in 1828. In 1829, he declared Sati a crime and abolished it. During Bentinck’s period, the Charter Act, 1833 was passed; it contained provisions aimed at abolishing slavery. Bentinck also launched a campaign against Thug gangs and tried to suppress them. He also worked on education and freedom of the press. In 1835, he returned to England. The provision of disqualification due to religious conversion was removed in 1850. Therefore, statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, and hence option (c) is the correct answer. Note—The Charter Act of 1833 was an initial and policy-level step towards the abolition of slavery, but slavery did not end immediately after the Act was passed. Rather, it provided a practical platform for abolition. The actual and formal abolition of slavery took place through the Indian Slavery Act, 1843. This Act directly declared the buying and selling of slaves, and keeping slaves, illegal.

questions.explanation: At the time of the Revolt of 1857, the Governor-General of India was Lord Canning (1856–58). Lord Canning was the last Governor-General appointed by the Company, and the first Viceroy of India appointed under the British Crown (1858–62).

questions.q: Which Viceroy adopted an aggressive policy towards Afghanistan?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Lord Lytton was not related to the Ilbert Bill controversy. The Ilbert Bill was introduced during the tenure of Viceroy Lord Ripon. This bill sought to allow senior Indian judges to try European offenders.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The tenure of Viceroy Lord Mayo (1869–72) is known for educational, economic and administrative reforms. Mayo issued a resolution on 14 December 1870. This resolution, for the first time, spoke of decentralizing the colonial economic structure and took the first step towards the division of central and provincial finances. It also granted some autonomy to provincial governments by allocating them a portion of central revenue for services like jails, education and medical facilities, and allowing them to administer as they wished. questions.q: Which of the following States was not annexed under Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.explanation: Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856) annexed Awadh into the British dominions in February 1856, accusing the Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah, of maladministration. Apart from Awadh, the territories annexed under Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse were—Satara (1849), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1854) and Nagpur (1854). Jaipur was not included in these. Under Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse, the process of annexation of Satara began in 1848, while it was completed on 1 May, 1849.

questions.q: The policy of 'Security Cell' is related to-
questions.explanation: The Ring-Fence Policy was associated with Warren Hastings and Wellesley. Warren Hastings fought wars with Mysore and the Marathas, and with other Indian states, with the aim of gaining an equal status. During this time, the Company tried to create buffer states around its territory. Its objective was only to protect its own state; or we can also say: “Protect the borders of your neighbouring states so that your own borders remain secure.” At that time, the main fear was from the Afghans and the Marathas. Therefore, the Company took charge of Awadh’s defence on the condition that the Nawab of Awadh would bear the expenditure; and in this way, the defence of Awadh was the defence of Bengal. With Wellesley’s arrival, the Company’s relations with Indian princely states changed. Wellesley’s objective was to compel Indian states to depend on the Company for their protection. He tried to bring Indian states within the ring of British political power and military protection.

questions.q: First Maratha Sardar to accept the subsidiary alliance of Lord Wellesley was-
questions.explanation: Daulat Rao Scindia and Jaswant Holkar both wanted to prove themselves supreme in Pune. Baji Rao II was supporting Scindia. In 1801, he got Jaswant’s brother killed; as a result, Jaswant Holkar’s army attacked Pune and defeated the combined forces of the Peshwa and Scindia. Baji Rao II fled and took refuge at Bassein, and on 31 December, 1802, he signed the Treaty of Bassein with the British. Under the treaty, Peshwa Baji Rao II accepted British protection. This treaty is regarded as the first Subsidiary Alliance concluded by the Marathas with the British.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870 are correct? 1. It was the first step that bifurcated Central and Provincial finances. 2. Provincial Governments were empowered to administer certain services. 3. It attempted to rectify existing imparity. 4. It focused on the actual needs of the Provinces. Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
questions.explanation: Viceroy Lord Mayo’s tenure (1869–1872) is remembered for his educational and administrative reforms. For administrative improvement, after correspondence with different administrations, he issued a resolution on 14 December, 1870, which is also called the “Mayo Resolution” or the “Charter of Provincial Governments.” It took the first step that bifurcated central and provincial finances; and while giving some autonomy to provincial governments, it allotted them funds from the central revenue for services like jails, education and medical services, and asked them to administer as they wished. In this way, Mayo promoted provincial autonomy and focused on the real needs of the provinces. In 1871, Mayo focused on financial decentralization and tried to balance the financial problems of the British Empire, which were marked by continuous deficits.

questions.q: When was the new Enfield Rifle with greased cartridges introduced in the British Indian Army?
questions.explanation: In December, 1856, the government decided to replace the old Brown Bess musket with the new Enfield rifle. Training for these rifles was to be given at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot. These rifles used greased cartridges, which were said to be coated with the fat of cows and pigs. In this rifle, the upper part of the cartridge had to be bitten off with the mouth. In January, 1857, a rumour spread in the Bengal Army that the greased cartridges contained the fat of cows and pigs. The military officers denied it immediately without proper investigation. But the soldiers became convinced that the use of such cartridges was a deliberate attempt to corrupt their religion, and this became the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857.

questions.q: Where from the Revolution of 1857 started first?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The incident of 24 April, 1857 at Meerut proved to be a milestone in the history of India’s freedom struggle. Colonel Carmichael Smyth ordered that greased cartridges be issued to Indian soldiers, which had to be opened with the mouth. Angered by this, 85 out of 90 soldiers of the 3rd Bengal Native Cavalry / 3rd Regiment of Light Cavalry revolted against these cartridges. On 9 May, 1857, these rebel soldiers were court-martialled at the Meerut parade ground. Enraged by this action, they revolted at Meerut on 10 May, 1857 and sounded the bugle of the first war of independence, i.e., the Revolt of 1857.

It is noteworthy that the incompetence of officers was not a cause, although ill-treatment by officers certainly aggravated the situation.

questions.q: The revolt of 1857 at Lucknow was led by :
questions.explanation: In Lucknow (Awadh), the revolt began on 30 May, 1857. It was led by the Begum of Awadh, Hazrat Mahal.

questions.q: Which of the following persons had participated actively in the Revolt of 1857?

options.E: None of the above/ More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The political, economic, social and religious causes, due to the Revolt of 1857 began. The revolt started in Lucknow in May, 1857 and it was led by Begum Hazrat Mahal. In Kanpur, it was led by Nana Saheb, and in Faizabad, it was led by Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah. On the other hand, the role of Begum Zeenat Mahal, wife of Bahadur Shah Zafar (the last Mughal emperor), in the Revolt of 1857 was doubtful. According to British sources, she was not a supporter of the rebels; rather, she sought a compromise with the British and acted in a way that weakened the revolt. However, some sources say that Zeenat Mahal opened the gates of Delhi for the rebels of 1857, but this claim is not confirmed by any reliable source. Therefore, among all the given options, the most appropriate answer is option (e).

The Poligars of Tamil Nadu revolted several times, and Dewan Velu Thampi of Travancore led a revolt against the English in 1808–09.

He was born in the Yeola/Yevla village of Maharashtra, where he became a friend of Nana Dhondu Pant (also known as Nana Saheb), the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II. questions.q: Which of the following groups did not participate in the revolt of 1857? 1. Agricultural Labour 2. Sahukar 3. Farmers 4. Zamindars Select your answer from the following codes :
questions.explanation: The Revolt of 1857 spread over a very large area and received wide popular support. Even so, it could not engulf the whole country or all sections and classes of Indian society. It did not spread to South India and to most parts of Eastern and Western India. Most rulers of the Indian princely states and the big zamindars were self-seeking and, frightened of British power, did not join the revolt. On the contrary, the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore, the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Maharaja of Jodhpur, the Sikh rulers of Patiala, Nabha and Jind, other Sikh chiefs of Punjab, the Maharaja of Kashmir, and many other chiefs and big zamindars actively helped the British in suppressing the revolt. Governor-General Canning later remarked that these rulers “acted like a dam before the storm; otherwise the storm would have swept us away in a single wave.” Traders and the educated class held meetings in Calcutta and Bombay and appealed to help the British. Most people of the upper and middle classes were critics of the rebels. Many talukdars (big zamindars) of Awadh who had joined the revolt withdrew from it after receiving an assurance from the British that their estates would be restored. In rural attacks, the main targets were moneylenders; therefore, they naturally became enemies of the revolt. Indians with modern education also did not support the revolt. The educated Indians wanted to remove the backwardness of the country. They were wrongly convinced that the British would help them in completing these tasks of modernization.

questions.q: What was the main cause of the failure of the revolt of 1857?

options.B: Lack of common strategy and central organization

questions.explanation: The main reason for the failure of the Revolt of 1857 was the lack of a common plan and a central organization. No spirit of organization was seen among the rebel leaders. The 82-year-old Bahadur Shah was weak, and his call to various chiefs was not sufficient. The rebels certainly showed bravery and appeared determined to destroy the government, but they completely lacked a planned and unified programme to do so. They also lacked discipline. At times, they behaved like a rioting mob rather than a disciplined army. Except for a shared hatred towards foreign rule, there was no other binding link among the leaders. After uprooting British authority from a particular region, they did not even know what kind of political power or institutions should be established in its place. They lacked a future-oriented programme, coherent ideology, political perspective, or a clear vision of a future society and economy.

questions.explanation: The Indigo Revolt began from Govindpur village in Nadia district of Bengal. Under the leadership of two former employees of an indigo planter—Digambar Biswas and Vishnu Biswas (Vishnucharan Biswas)—the peasants united there and stopped cultivating indigo. This was the most widespread and militant revolt in the history of indigo movements in terms of demands. The Indigo Revolt of Bengal was the peasants’ direct struggle against exploitation. The cultivators of Bengal who wanted to grow rice in their fields were forced by European indigo planters to cultivate indigo. Those who refused indigo cultivation had to face the oppressive machinery of the planters. In March 1859, thousands of raiyats in Bengal refused to cultivate indigo. As the revolt spread, the raiyats also refused to pay rent to the planters. By 1860, the indigo movement spread to Nadia, Pabna, Khulna, Dhaka, Malda, Dinajpur, etc. Due to the unity of the peasants, by 1860 almost all indigo factories in Bengal were closed. The intellectual class of Bengal expressed support for this revolt through newspaper articles and public meetings. The editor of “Hindu Patriot,” Harishchandra Mukherjee, played a special role in it. The atrocities of indigo planters were vividly portrayed by Dinabandhu Mitra in his play “Neel Darpan.”

The main causes of the revolt were the British government’s attempts to ban human sacrifice (Meriah), the imposition of new taxes, and the entry of zamindars and moneylenders into many areas, which caused immense suffering to the tribals. questions.q: Consider the following statements regarding Wood’s Dispatch of 1854 : 1. It recommended English as the medium of instruction for higher studies. 2. It laid stress on female education and vocational training. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: In 1854, the Court of Directors of the East India Company in London sent a note to the Governor-General of India, Lord Dalhousie, on the subject of education. In response, Charles Wood, the President of the Board of Control, issued a policy document in July 1854, which is known as ‘Wood’s Despatch’ or ‘Wood’s policy document/charter’. This charter prepared a comprehensive plan for future education in India, and it is called the ‘Magna Carta’ of English education in India. Wood’s Despatch made the following recommendations— (i) Emphasis was laid on imparting higher education through the medium of the English language; however, importance was also given to the development of vernacular (native) languages. (ii) It recommended women’s education and vocational training. (iv) Establishment of one university each in the three Presidencies (Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras) on the model of the University of London. questions.q: To control the media in India, ‘Acts’ were passed in –
questions.explanation: To control newspapers that exposed the government’s repressive policies, the Press Act of 1835 (Act No. XI of 1835) was promulgated. After this, the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 was passed. Viceroy Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878, under which no newspaper could be published without the government’s permission if it contained criticism of the British government. In addition, an Act to control the press was passed by Lord Minto in 1908, under which the government had the power to confiscate any publication that was accused of inciting public feeling against the government.

questions.q: Who among the following repealed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
questions.explanation: Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882 and gave Indian-language newspapers the same freedom as English-language newspapers. It is noteworthy that the Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878 during Lord Lytton’s tenure (1876–1880). This Act was called the “Gagging Act.” Its most objectionable feature was that it discriminated between newspapers in Indian languages and those in English, and it did not give the offender the right to appeal. Under this Act, a district magistrate, or the Police Commissioner of a presidency town—within whose local jurisdiction a newspaper was printed and published—had the power to make any Indian-language newspaper sign a bond (Bond) stating that it would not publish any antigovernment material. The security deposit of printing presses that opposed the law could be cancelled. Under this Act, cases were registered against Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, Sahchar, and many other newspapers.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Vernacular Press Act is/are correct? 1. It was enacted by Lord Lytton. 2. It came to be known as a ‘Gagging Act’. 3. The Act was repealed by Lord Ripon. Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
questions.explanation: Lord Lytton enacted the Vernacular Press Act, 1878, which empowered the government to seize newspapers publishing so-called “anti-government material”. It may be noted that English-language newspapers were exempted from this Act and were not regulated under its provisions. Under the Vernacular Press Act, any magistrate or police commissioner had the authority to order any printer or publisher of a newspaper not to print a specified kind of material and could seize any printed matter considered objectionable. This Act was nicknamed the “Gagging Act”. Its most objectionable features were—(i) discrimination between the English and vernacular press, and (ii) no right of appeal. Under the VPA, action was initiated against newspapers such as Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, and others. This law was repealed in 1882 by Lord Ripon (Viceroy, 1880–84), Lord Lytton’s successor.

questions.explanation: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission on 1 May 1897 in memory of his guru. After taking sannyasa, he made an extensive study of religious scriptures. Swami Vivekananda emerged as a propagator of this Neo-Hinduism. In 1893, he went to Chicago, where he delivered his famous speech at the ‘Parliament of the World’s Religions’ (World Parliament of Religions). Through this speech, for the first time, he presented the importance of India’s culture before the Western world in a very effective manner. After this, he travelled in America and England and propagated Hinduism. Swamiji strongly condemned the tendency in Hinduism that says, “Don’t touchism.” According to him, Hinduism had now become confined only to food and drink. He was very unhappy with religion’s silence on the exploitation of the poor by the rich. According to him, to speak of religion to a hungry person is an insult to God and humanity. Vivekananda did not give any political message; yet, through his writings and speeches, he awakened in the new generation a renewed sense of self-respect in their past. He was a true patriot. Subhas Chandra Bose said about him: “As far as Bengal is concerned, we may look upon Vivekananda as the ‘Spiritual Father’ of the modern national movement.”

questions.q: Dayanand Saraswati founded –
questions.explanation: Dayanand Saraswati (Mool Shankar) founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875, whose main objective was to re-establish the ancient Vedic religion in its pure form. In the religious sphere, he did not accept idol worship, polytheism, avatarism, animal sacrifice, blind faith, tantra-mantra, and false rituals. He considered the Vedas as divine knowledge and accepted literature up to the Upanishadic period. The rules and principles of the Arya Samaj were first framed in Bombay; later, they were edited in Lahore in 1877 and given a definite form. The expansion of Arya Samaj was highly successful in Punjab, and to some extent it also achieved success in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Rajasthan. Mahatma Hansraj, Pandit Gurudutt, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Swami Shraddhanand were among its notable workers. In 1893, the Arya Samaj split into two groups—one group supported Western education, while the other opposed it. Among the opponents of Western education, Swami Shraddhanand (another name—Mahatma Munshiram) and Lekhram were prominent. These people founded ‘Gurukul Kangri’ (Gurukul Kangri University) in 1902. Among the supporters of Western education, Lala Lajpat Rai and Hansraj were prominent. These people founded the ‘Dayanand Anglo-Vedic College’.

They could not realise that their very achievements had made their politics impractical. questions.q: Who was the President of the Indian National Congress at the time of the partition of India?

options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: When India became independent, J.B. Kripalani was the President of the Congress. He was elected President at the Meerut Session of the Congress (November 1946), and he remained President at the time of Independence as well. The Jaipur Session of the Congress (December 1948) was presided over by Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Mahatma Gandhi presided over the Belgaum Session (1924); Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore, Lucknow and Faizpur Sessions (respectively: December 1929, April 1936 and December 1936); and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel presided over the Karachi Session (March 1931).

questions.q: Who presided over the Delhi Session the of Indian National Congress in 1947?
questions.explanation: A special session of the Indian National Congress was held in Delhi on 14–15 June 1947. Although Acharya J.B. Kripalani was the President of the Congress then, this historic meeting was presided over by Dr. Rajendra Prasad. The main purpose of this meeting was to deliberate on the Mountbatten Plan.

questions.q: At the Congress Working Committee meeting at Allahabad (April-May 1947), who of the following members was able to secure a majority for his plan of a guerrilla War against the Japanese due to India’s unequivocal stand against Nazism, Fascism and imperialism?

questions.q: In which of the following Indian National Congress Sessions, the resolutions related to the Fundamental Rights were passed for the first time?
questions.explanation: To approve the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact), the Karachi Session of the Congress was held on 29–31 March 1931 under the presidentship of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. In this session, for the first time, the Congress passed resolutions related to Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme. In the same session, when some people opposed it, Gandhiji said, “Gandhi may die, but Gandhism will not.”

questions.q: Which Indian leader for the first time used the 'Safety- Valve Theory'to attack the Moderates in the Congress?
questions.explanation: For the first time, the extremist leader Lala Lajpat Rai, in his book Young India published in 1916, used this theory to accuse the moderate leaders of the Congress of running an organisation which the British rulers were using like a “safety-valve”.

questions.q: Most of the moderate leaders hailed from :
questions.explanation: In the era of liberal politics or political mendicancy, most moderate leaders—such as Dadabhai Naoroji, Ferozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee and Surendranath Banerjee—were associated with urban areas. During this period, the Congress was dominated by prosperous, middle-class intellectuals, including lawyers, doctors, engineers, journalists and literary persons. Titles and high positions attracted them. The representatives who came to the Congress generally came from big cities, and their contact with the common people was limited. Ferozeshah Mehta himself said, “The voice of the Congress is not the voice of the people; however, it is the duty of other countrymen living among them to understand their feelings.

questions.q: Which one of the following was not an extremist?
questions.explanation: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was associated with the Liberal (Moderate) camp. He believed in equanimity and a gentle sense of justice. He had complete faith that the nation’s regeneration could not take place amid storms of agitation. He believed in the purity of both means and ends. Influenced by these ideas, Gandhiji became his disciple. He entered politics from the platform of the Bombay Congress session of 1889. In 1897, he and Dinshaw Wacha were asked to give evidence before the Welby Commission appointed to examine Indian expenditure. In 1899, he was elected to the Bombay Legislative Council and later to the Imperial Legislative Council.

questions.q: Indian National Movement came to be dominated by the extremists after –
questions.explanation: After 1906, within the Congress, the influence of the extremist group increased in Indian politics. The extremist group was jointly led by major Congress leaders—Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Aurobindo Ghosh.

questions.q: Which one of the following leaders belonged to the Extremist wing of the Congress?
questions.explanation: Aurobindo Ghosh was a leader of the extremist group in the Congress. He was one of the four pillars of the extremist group (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Aurobindo Ghosh). In his article written in 1893–94, he said that the Congress was away from the working class, was anti-national, and had completely failed; and he described as cowardice the Congress policy of not speaking clearly due to fear of displeasing the British rulers. According to him, the Congress was going to die of tuberculosis. In 1908, the police raided Manictala Garden (another name—Murari Pukur Baganbari), arrested 14 revolutionaries, and arrested Aurobindo Ghosh from his house on Grey Street. All of them were tried in the Alipore Conspiracy Case. The trial against Aurobindo Ghosh continued for about a year, but later he was acquitted due to lack of evidence. In the course of time, he withdrew from revolutionary activities, became an ascetic, and went to Pondicherry (now Puducherry).

questions.q: Who propounded the doctrine of ‘Passive Resistance’?
questions.explanation: A series of articles on “Passive Resistance” was first published in the newspaper Bande Mataram between 9 and 23 April, 1907. Aurobindo Ghosh believed that the British should leave India immediately. Until the British did so, protests against them should continue.

questions.q: Who among the following was not known as a moderate in the National Movement?
questions.explanation: Among the four main pillars of extremism (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Aurobindo Ghosh), Bal Gangadhar Tilak was the pioneer of this ideology. He criticized the Congress policy of petition and prayer. Tilak said about the Congress, “If we croak like frogs once a year, we will get nothing.” Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale were Moderate leaders of the Congress, whereas M.G. Ranade was a social reformer.

questions.q: Bal Gangadhar Tilak came to be known as 'Lokmanya Tilak' when –

options.C: The government accused him in the Rand Murder Case.
options.D: He started the Shivaji and Ganpati festivals.
options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above.

questions.explanation: The British government made Bal Gangadhar Tilak an accused in the murder case of the then Pune plague commissioner W.C. Rand and Lieutenant Ayerst. Tilak was found guilty and was sentenced to 18 months of rigorous imprisonment. When he came out of jail, he emerged as a national hero. Thus, not due to any single incident, but after many nationalist actions, Tilak was given the title “Lokmanya.”

questions.q: Who said, “Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it”?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The slogan, “Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it,” associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, has been a subject of considerable disagreement among scholars regarding when Tilak first used it. In fact, the idea of this slogan began to take shape in the 1890s. Scholars believe that Tilak’s close associate, Joseph “Kaka” Baptista, first coined this sentence. It is believed that Baptista probably composed this line in Marathi—“Swarajya ha maza janmasiddha hakk ahe, ani to mi milavnarach”—and Tilak adopted it and carried it to the masses. On the basis of available evidence, it can be said that Tilak used this slogan from public platforms during the Home Rule Movement in April–May 1916. Some sources emphasize that Tilak used this slogan at the Lucknow session of the Congress in 1916, but sufficient historical evidence in support of this is not available.

questions.q: Which movement was started as a reaction to the Partition of Bengal?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon, announced the Partition of Bengal on 19 July 1905 (some sources also mention 20 July 1905). In protest against this announcement, a historic meeting was held at the Calcutta Town Hall, where the formal declaration was made of the Swadeshi Movement. When the Partition of Bengal was implemented in October 1905, that day was observed as a “Day of Mourning”. On the suggestion of Rabindranath Tagore, it was also observed as “Rakhi Day”. Nationalists observed this day to demonstrate the unbroken unity of Bengal. On the lines of Tagore’s Shantiniketan, the Bengal National College was established. Very soon, many national schools were set up across the country. In March 1906, the National Council of Education was formed. The Swadeshi Movement raised the slogan of self-reliance and self-power. The question of self-support and self-reliance was linked with national self-respect, honour, and self-confidence. The Congress, in its Calcutta Session (1906), also passed four resolutions related to the Swadeshi Movement, the Boycott Movement, National Education, and Self-government. Thus, it is clear that in opposition to the Partition of Bengal, nationalists launched movements such as Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, and Self-government.

questions.q: In which year partition of Bengal made by Lord Curzon was cancelled?
questions.explanation: In December 1911, on the arrival of King-Emperor George V and Queen Mary in India, a Durbar was held in Delhi to welcome them. At the Delhi Durbar, on 12 December 1911, the King-Emperor declared the annulment of the Partition of Bengal. He also announced that Delhi would be made the new capital of India in place of Calcutta. In accordance with this announcement, Bengal was reorganised as a new province. Orissa and Bihar were separated from it. Assam was made a new province, as it had been in 1874, and Sylhet was added to it.

questions.q: Who among the following was the founder of the All India Muslim League?
questions.explanation: In October 1906, under the leadership of Aga Khan, the Simla Deputation of Muslims proposed the idea of forming a central Muslim organization to protect Muslim interests. In line with this idea, during the All India Mohammedan Educational Conference held at Dhaka in December 1906, Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dhaka the President of the reception committee of the conference and the convenor of political meetings got a resolution passed for the formation of the All India Muslim League. A 60-member provisional committee was selected, and Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Waqarul-Mulk were appointed jointly as Secretaries of the organization. The headquarters of the Muslim League was set up at Lucknow, and Aga Khan was made its first President. In the options, if these three names are present (or if any two of them are present), then the order of preference for selecting the “founder” will be as follows— 1.Salimullah Khan 2. Aga Khan 3. Mohsin-ul-Mulk. Since the first two names are given in the present question, Salimullah Khan will be selected as the founder by giving him first preference.

In 1907, the annual session of the Muslim League was held at Karachi, and in 1908 at Amritsar. After this, the sessions of the Muslim League continued to be held irregularly in different cities. However, the Bihar Public Service Commission, in its answer key, considered option (d) as the answer to this question, which is not correct.

The deputation demanded a special position for Muslims for elections in provincial, central, and local bodies. In response to this demand, Minto assured the Muslims that their political rights and interests would be protected in India.

questions.q: Which of the following Acts introduced the separate electorate system in India?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Through the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley–Minto Reforms, 1909), a system of communal representation was introduced in British India, under which provision was made for separate electorates for Muslims.

questions.explanation: H. S. Olcott was associated not with the Home Rule League, but with the Theosophical Society. After this, he enrolled in Samaldas Arts College, Bhavnagar. After that, he completed his studies in Law from University College London.

After returning to India in 1915, Mahatma Gandhi began his political life in India under the guidance of Gokhale.

questions.q: Who first used the word "Sarvodaya"?'
questions.explanation: Sarvodaya is formed from two Sanskrit words—sarva (meaning: all) and udaya (meaning: upliftment). The word Sarvodaya was used for the first time by Mahatma Gandhi. In 1908, it was used in the translation of John Ruskin’s book ‘Unto This Last’. Its objective was to develop the spirit of freedom and equality in everyone. Note—In the book ‘Mahavira: His Times and Philosophy of Life’ written by Dr. Hiralal Jain and A. N. Upadhyay, it is written that the word ‘Sarvodaya’ was first used by a Jain philosopher named Samantabhadra around the 2nd century BCE. Later, Gandhiji gave this word a strong foundation and made it popular among the masses.

questions.q: Which of the following was Gandhiji's first Satyagraha Movement in India in which he used civil disobedience?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Champaran Movement (1917) was Gandhiji’s first Satyagraha movement in India, in which he used civil disobedience. This Satyagraha was started as a protest against the ‘Tinkathia system’ prevalent in Champaran (Bihar) in the early 19th century. After the Champaran Satyagraha, Gandhiji used Satyagraha in 1918 when he intervened in the dispute between the cotton mill owners and workers in Ahmedabad over the plague bonus. In the same year, 1918, Gandhiji started the Kheda Satyagraha in Gujarat because, despite crops being destroyed, the British government did not grant remission in land revenue. It may be noted that Gandhiji began the Rowlatt Satyagraha in 1919 in protest against the ‘Rowlatt Act’ passed by the British government.

questions.q: Who invited Gandhiji to come to Champaran?

options.E: None of the above More than one of the above

questions.explanation: After returning from South Africa in January 1915, Gandhiji carried out his first successful Satyagraha in Bihar’s Champaran district in 1917. In 1916, a Champaran farmer, Rajkumar Shukla, met Gandhiji in Lucknow and urged him to visit Champaran. The Champaran issue was quite old. By the end of the 19th century, German synthetic dyes replaced indigo in the market. As a result, the European plantation owners in Champaran were forced to stop indigo cultivation. The peasants too wanted to get rid of indigo cultivation as a cash crop. Taking advantage of the peasants helplessness, the white planters arbitrarily increased rent and other illegal taxes in the name of releasing them from their contracts. It was against this exploitation of the peasants that Gandhiji began the Champaran Satyagraha.

The formation of this committee was the outcome of an agreement reached between Gandhiji and the then government.

questions.q: In response to the mass agitation of the Champaran Movement, the British Government took which step to address the issue?

options.A: Appointed Mahatma Gandhi as the Governor of Champaran
options.B: Enforced strict curfew and imposed Martial Law in the region
options.D: Declared Champaran as an independent State

questions.explanation: To resolve the Champaran Satyagraha (1917), the British government appointed an inquiry committee to investigate the agrarian conditions of Champaran. Gandhiji was chosen as a member of this committee. On the basis of the committee’s recommendations, the British government passed the Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918. Under this Act, the Champaran Agrarian Committee was established.

questions.q: When was Mahatma Gandhi prosecuted for the Champaran Satyagraha?

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In 1917, Mahatma Gandhi was prosecuted for the Champaran Satyagraha. Gandhiji carried out his first major experiment of Satyagraha in 1917 in the Champaran district of Bihar. N. G. Ranga opposed Mahatma Gandhi’s Champaran Satyagraha. A few years after the Champaran Satyagraha, Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore addressed Gandhiji as “Mahatma”. However, no authentic primary source is available that mentions Rabindranath Tagore addressing Gandhiji as “Mahatma” during the Champaran Satyagraha.

questions.q: The person not connected with Champaran movement was-

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The peasants had to cultivate indigo on at least 3/20 of their land and sell it at prices fixed by the European planters. This was also called the Tinkathia system. If the peasants wanted exemption from indigo cultivation, they had to pay compensation, which was called “Tawan”.

questions.q: Who participated in ‘Satyagraha’ started by Gandhiji at Ahmedabad in 1917-18?
questions.explanation: After the success at Champaran, Gandhiji’s next experiment was to intervene in 1918 in a dispute in a cotton textile mill in Ahmedabad between the mill owners and the workers regarding an increase in bonus. The dispute was over the plague bonus. After the plague subsided, the owners wanted to discontinue it, while the workers demanded that it should continue. After a detailed study of production cost, profits, and the workers’ subsistence expenses, Gandhiji declared that the workers’ wages should be increased by 35%. The tribunal constituted by the mill owners accepted his view.

Andrews—Banarsidas Chaturvedi and Marjorie Sykes—in their book “Charles Freer Andrews: A Narrative” mention that the nickname “Deenbandhu” (friend of the poor) was first given to C.F. options.B: High interest rates charged by Mahajans
options.E: None of the above above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Deccan Riots of 1875 had many causes, such as: high interest rates charged by Mahajans and peasants becoming permanently indebted; high interest rates related to land revenue; getting peasants to sign loan documents by mortgaging their fields, houses, etc., due to illiteracy and poverty; and the failure of peasants to protect their interests due to the complex and costly judicial system. The Bihar Public Service Commission considered option (b) as the correct answer.

questions.explanation: In 1921–22, the peasants of Awadh ran a movement known as the Eka Movement. This movement was concentrated in the Hardoi, Bahraich, Barabanki, and Sitapur regions. The chief leader of the Eka Movement was Madari Pasi.

questions.q: What was the aim of Eka Movement in Oudh?

options.A: To stop to giving rent to the Government
options.B: To protect the rights of landlords

questions.explanation: The Eka Movement (1921–22) was led by Madari Pasi. The main centres of this movement were Hardoi, Barabanki, Bahraich and Sitapur. The peasants main complaints were the increase in land revenue and the practice of collecting land revenue in the form of produce. More than 50% land revenue was being taken from the peasants. The zamindars’ agents (thekedars) used to harass the peasants. The Eka Movement had little faith in the non-violent policies laid down by the nationalists. As a result, the nationalist leaders became separated from the movement, and the movement took a different path. In this movement, paying land revenue to the government was not stopped; rather, the main demand of the agitators was—“Due to rising inflation, land revenue should be converted into cash payment.”

chapters.chapter_name: Rowlatt Act And Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

questions.q: When was the Rowlatt Act passed?
questions.explanation: To curb the rising revolutionary activities in India, the government constituted a committee in 1917 under the chairmanship of Justice Sidney Rowlatt, with the objective of preparing an effective plan to suppress terrorism. On the basis of its recommendations, the bill passed in March, 1919 came to be known as the Rowlatt Act. Under the Rowlatt Act, the British government could imprison anyone, without trial, for a maximum of two years. Therefore, this law was called the law of “No appeal, No dalil, No Vakil”.

questions.q: Indian National Congress opposed the Rowlatt Act because it aimed-

options.B: To ban the Indian National Congress
options.D: To imprison national leaders charging the traitors to the nation

questions.explanation: The bill passed by the Central Legislative Council in March, 1919 was known as the Rowlatt Act. According to it, the British government could imprison anyone, without trial, for a maximum of two years. This law limited individual liberty.

questions.explanation: On 31 December 1922, in a meeting held at the residence of the Maharaja of Tikari in Gaya, the formation of a new party within the Congress—‘Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party’ was announced. In 1923, the ‘Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party’ (Swaraj Party) was formed, and from 20–22 February 1923, the general meeting of this newly formed party was held in Allahabad (present-day Prayagraj). In this meeting, the party’s programme and constitution were approved and the party was given the new name ‘Swaraj Party’. C.R. Das became its President and Motilal Nehru became its General Secretary. This party was formed with the objective of contesting council elections while remaining within the Congress. It also participated in the elections to the State Councils as well as the Central Legislative Council and achieved good success. Their real aim was to enter these assemblies, present their views, and practise non-cooperation with the government from within. The Swaraj Party was established after the failure of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

questions.q: When did Simon Commission visit India?
questions.explanation: In the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms of 1919, there was a provision to set up a Statutory Commission for review after 10 years. The Commission had to examine how far this Act had been successful in practice and how much progress had been made towards responsible government. However, the Conservative government in Britain appointed the Simon Commission (Indian Statutory Commission) two years earlier itself, in November 1927. This commission was chaired by Sir John Simon and had a total of 7 members. Since all the members were British, the Congressmen opposed it by calling it a “White Commission.” The Simon Commission reached Bombay on 3 February 1928.

options.A: Motilal Nehru and Jawaharlal Nehru; India’s relationship with the British Empire
options.B: Jawaharlal Nehru; local self-government in India

options.D: Jawaharlal Nehru; constitutional arrangements in India

questions.explanation: Since no Indian was included in the Simon Commission, during the protests against the Commission in India, the Secretary of State for India, Lord Birkenhead, challenged the Indians and said that Indians were incapable of making concrete proposals for constitutional reforms. He said that Indians were unable to frame a constitution that could receive broad political support from all Indians. The Indians accepted this challenge, and to finalize this plan, all-party conferences were held in February, May and August, 1928. A committee of nine members under the chairmanship of Motilal Nehru (the total number of members, including the chairman, was 10) presented the draft of the proposed constitution in August, 1928. Later, it came to be known as the “Nehru Report” after Motilal Nehru. In it, the demand for separate electorates on a communal basis was rejected. This report demanded “Dominion Status”. Besides this, other recommendations were also made, such as: adult franchise for all, equal rights for women, freedom to form unions (associations), and separation of religion from the state in every respect.

questions.explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru said in Lahore: “Remember once again, now that this flag is unfurled; it must not be lowered as long as a single Indian man, woman, or child remains alive in India.” The Lahore Session of 1929 was presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. In this very session, the resolution of “Purna Swaraj” was passed, and it was decided to celebrate 26 January as Independence Day.

questions.q: The proposal of Purna Swaraj was passed in Lahore Congress in the year-
questions.explanation: In the Calcutta Session of the Congress, an ultimatum was given to the British Government that it should accept the Nehru Report by the end of the year, or else it would have to face a mass movement to be started by the Congress. When the government did not give any definite reply within the fixed time-limit, the historic Lahore Session of the Congress was held in December, 1929 under the presidentship of Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru, in which Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru declared the objective of Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence). As the midnight hour struck on 31 December, 1929, the Congress President, Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru, unfurled the flag of Indian independence on the banks of the Ravi River at Lahore. In its meeting on 2 January, 1930, the Congress Working Committee decided that 26 January, 1930 would be celebrated as “Purna Swadhinata Diwas” or “Purna Swaraj Diwas”. From here, the celebration of 26 January every year as Complete Independence Day began.

questions.q: Dandi March was undertaken in :

questions.q: The Provincial Governments were constituted under the Act of-
questions.explanation: On the basis of the Government of India Act, 1935, elections to the provincial legislatures were held in February 1937. In these elections, Congress wiped out its rival parties and secured an absolute majority in five provinces—Madras (159 out of 215 seats), Bihar (98 out of 152), Central Provinces and Berar (70 out of 112), United Provinces (134 out of 228), and Orissa (36 out of 60). Congress emerged as the largest party in Bombay (almost an absolute majority), Assam, and the North-West Frontier Province. Only in Bengal, Punjab, and Sind was Congress unable to become the largest party. In July 1937, Congress formed its governments in 6 provinces—Madras, United Provinces, Central Provinces and Berar, Bihar, Bombay, and Orissa. Note: In Bombay, Congress got almost an absolute majority (86 out of 175 seats). In Ayodhya Singh’s book 'Bharat Ka Mukti-Sangram', Congress is shown as having an absolute majority in Bombay as well (88 out of 175 seats), which, according to other sources, is not correct.

At the Tripuri session of 1939, he became President for the second time by defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya, who was supported by Gandhiji; however, due to differences with Gandhiji on the issue of constituting the Working Committee, he resigned, after which Dr. Rajendra Prasad became the acting President of Congress. It should be noted that the Second World War ended (especially with reference to Japan’s surrender) in August–September 1945 (in August 1945, the United States of America dropped atomic bombs on Japan, and in September 1945 Japan signed the surrender instrument). During this period (August–September 1945), Clement Attlee was the Prime Minister of Britain, not Churchill. After the change of power in Britain in July 1945, Attlee (1945–1951) became Prime Minister in place of Churchill. In an official research note of the British Parliament (House of Lords Library), it is clearly stated that the confirmation of the end of the Second World War was made through a radio broadcast by Prime Minister Attlee.

options.D: Improvement of relationships between Indian Provinces and the Crown.

questions.explanation: The Butler Committee was constituted in 1927; it is also called the Indian States Committee. Its objective was to examine the relations between the Government of India and the Indian princely states, and to make recommendations to improve the economic and financial relations between British India and the princely states. The Indian rulers appointed a well-known lawyer, Leslie Scott, to present their viewpoint before the Committee. Scott argued that each princely state was originally independent, and therefore it remained independent except to the extent to which it had surrendered its sovereignty to the British Crown; that is, special rights/ privileges lay with the princely states.

questions.q: Who raised the cry "Divide and Quit"
questions.explanation: The slogan “Divide and Quit” was raised by the Muslim League leader Muhammad Ali Jinnah during the Second World War, in 1943. Jinnah and the Muslim League demanded that the British should first divide India into two parts—Hindustan and Pakistan—and then quit India. This idea was expressed in the form of the political slogan “Divide and Quit”.

questions.q: Who among following led the movement for the separate State of Pakistan?
questions.explanation: On 22–24 March, 1940, the Muslim League session was held at Lahore. It was presided over by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. In this session, a resolution was passed demanding ‘independent states’ for the Muslims of the north-western and eastern regions; this is known as the ‘Lahore Resolution’. Later, this ‘Lahore Resolution’ came to be known as the ‘Pakistan Resolution’. However, it is noteworthy that this resolution mentioned neither partition nor the word ‘Pakistan’. In the Lahore Resolution, it was stated that separate independent states should be formed by grouping together the Muslimmajority regions of north-western and eastern India—not a single independent nation. Some people at that time interpreted it as a demand for two independent countries (India and Pakistan). However, the Lahore Resolution (Pakistan Resolution) later paved the way for the creation of Pakistan.

questions.q: Who viewed the Cripps proposal as a 'post-dated cheque upon a crashing bank'?

questions.q: Quit India movement began on:
questions.explanation: On 7–8 August 1942, a special meeting of the All India Congress Committee was held at the historic Gowalia Tank (August Kranti Maidan) in Bombay, in which the Wardha Resolution (Quit India) was ratified. After minor amendments, the resolution was adopted on 8 August 1942, and the formal launch of the Quit India Movement against the British, as part of India’s freedom struggle, took place on 8 August 1942 itself. On 9 August 1942, due to the arrest of leaders, the movement spontaneously spread among the masses. Thus, the practical beginning of the Quit India Movement is considered to be 9 August 1942. As soon as the movement began, under “Operation Zero Hour”, Gandhiji and other prominent Congress leaders were arrested. Gandhiji was arrested and kept in the Aga Khan Palace at Poona (Pune) along with Sarojini Naidu. The 1942 movement had the maximum impact in Bombay, Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, the United Provinces and Madras.

After minor amendments, the resolution was adopted on 8 August 1942, and the formal launch of the Quit India Movement against the British, as part of India’s freedom struggle, took place on 8 August 1942 itself. On 9 August 1942, due to the arrest of leaders, the movement spontaneously spread among the masses. Thus, the practical beginning of the Quit India Movement is considered to be 9 August 1942. Gandhiji was arrested and kept in the Aga Khan Palace at Poona (Pune) along with Sarojini Naidu. questions.q: "We shall either free India or die in the attempt "who said it?
questions.explanation: This statement was made by Mahatma Gandhi on 8 August 1942 on the occasion of the Quit India Movement. In his speech, he said that Indians must now resolve that either they will make India free, or they will sacrifice their lives in this effort.

questions.q: Quit India Movement was led by :

questions.q: The slogan ‘Do or Die’ was related with –

Jatiya Sarkar — Tamluk (Bengal) — In Tamluk (Bengal), Jatiya Sarkar was established, which was a strong parallel government during the Quit India Movement. questions.q: Who formed the Forward Bloc?
questions.explanation: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was born on 23 January 1897 in Cuttack, Odisha. questions.q: In which year was the Indian National Army founded?
questions.explanation: In practical terms, as a military unit, the Indian National Army (another name—Azad Hind Fauj) was formed on 15 July 1942 under the leadership of Captain Mohan Singh, while the Bangkok Conference resolutions of June 1942 paved the way for the formation of the INA (Indian National Army). It is noteworthy that Indian residents in the Malaya region formed a political organisation named the “All Malaya Indian Independence League”. Rash Bihari Bose was invited to preside over it. In the Bangkok Conference held in June 1942, a proposal was made to form a “Council of Action” and a “Representative Committee”, which was entrusted with the responsibility of coordination and supervision between the “Indian Independence League” and the “Indian National Army”. Rash Behari Bose was made the Chairman of the Council of Action, while K. P. K. Menon and Nedyam Raghavan were civilian members, and Mohan Singh and Gilani were military members. Due to ideological differences with the Japanese, Mohan Singh announced the dissolution of the INA in December 1942; however, Rash Behari Bose removed Mohan Singh from his post. Later, Mohan Singh was arrested by the Japanese army. The leadership of the INA was handed over by Rash Bihari Bose to the great leader Subhas Chandra Bose. Two days after reaching Singapore, on 4 July 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose assumed the leadership of the Indian National Army. For convenience, it is also called the Second Indian National Army. In Hindi, we know it as the “Azad Hind Fauj.”

questions.q: In October 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose set up a provisional government of Free India which was recognized by how many countries including Japan?
questions.explanation: In October 1943, during the Second World War, the Provisional Government of Azad Hind (Provisional Government of Free India) established by Subhas Chandra Bose was recognized by nine countries. These were mainly Axis powers and Japan-backed regimes. The list of recognizing countries is as follows- 1. Japan, 2. Germany (Nazi regime), 3. Italy, 4. Thailand (Siam), 5. Burma/Myanmar (Japan-supported government), 6. Philippines (Second Republic sponsored by Japan), 7. Manchukuo (Japanese puppet government in Manchuria, China), 8. Wang Jingwei regime (Nanjing, China—Japanese puppet government), and 9. Croatia (a puppet government supported by powers). Some sources mention Slovakia or some other Axis-associated country, but the widely accepted number is nine. However, these recognitions were largely symbolic. Note- The Wang Jingwei regime is also called the Nationalist China or China (Nanking/Nanjing) regime.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: On 20 February 1947, Attlee stated before the House of Commons that his government intended to transfer power to Indians by June 1948. He also said that if by then no decision on a constitution had been reached, the British Government would have to consider to whom the powers of the central government in British India should be handed over—either to a central government, or to provincial governments in some areas, or in any other manner considered appropriate in the interests of the Indian people. In March 1947, Lord Mountbatten was sworn in as Viceroy. His task was to wind up British power in India. He was specifically instructed to keep India united as far as possible along with the transfer of power; however, he was also authorised to take decisions according to the changed circumstances in India so that Britain could withdraw honourably with minimum loss. Mountbatten soon reached the conclusion during the talks on the transfer of power that the partition of India and the creation of Pakistan had become necessary.
